findings.element: the container query @container (min-width: 600px) at b.css:1111 governing .b-print .b-two, plus [data-medium="sheet"] .b-print { padding: 56px 64px 44px } at b.css:1158, rendered at true A4 (794x1123 CSS px at 96dpi)
findings.problem: Driven at real A4 for the first time. At 794x1123 the keepsake's content box measures 584px wide: 794 less the stage's 80 less the field's 128 of padding. The container query that turns the keepsake into the two-column composition every frame and every panel round has looked at fires at 600. It misses by sixteen pixels. So at the size it is actually printed, grid-template-columns resolves to a single 584px track: the horizon stacks ABOVE the measure instead of standing beside it, the document runs 1935px against A4's 1123, and page.pdf({format:"A4"}) returns two pages, not one. Sheet two carries the 65-day row, the 79-day row, the whole behind-you block, the URL line and the footer, so on the only artifact this product makes that cannot be reflowed after it exists, the wedding day is on the back. There is no @page rule and zero break-inside, break-after or page-break declarations anywhere in shell.css or b.css: I enumerated every rule in every sheet under print media and the set is empty. Today's break lands at y1123, in a blank stretch of rail between Final guest numbers ending at 1092 and Venue walk-through starting at 1192, so nothing straddles it - by luck, on one fixture. Any plan whose dates fall differently gets a row sliced through the middle. The 1440 frame at shots/approach-print--1440x960.png shows a 220 + 396 two-column sheet; that sheet is a screen picture of a document no printer will ever produce.
findings.fix: Move the threshold below the real number and make the page a page. In b.css:1111 change the query to @container (min-width: 560px), and set b.css:1158 to [data-medium="sheet"] .b-print { padding: 48px 48px 40px } so the A4 content box widens from 584 to 616 and clears the threshold with margin rather than by a hair. Append to b.css: @page { size: A4; margin: 0 } and @media print { .tl-stage, .tl-paperEdge { max-width: none; padding: 0; border: 0 } .b-item, .b-behindRow, .b-behindSummary, .b-printLink, .b-foot { break-inside: avoid } .b-behind, .b-foot { break-before: avoid } }. With the horizon back beside the measure the sheet lands near 1050px at SCALE.print = 10; if a longer plan overruns, drop SCALE.print to 8 rather than letting it spill. Gate it: add a case to interaction-check.mjs that loads state=print at 794x1123 and fails if document.documentElement.scrollHeight exceeds 1123, or if getComputedStyle on .b-two returns a single-track grid-template-columns. Nobody should be able to ship a two-sheet keepsake again without the gate saying so.

findings.element: the min-width: 1280px desk query in b.css governing .b-two's grid, the horizon's position: sticky and .b-todayRule's width, driven at 701, 900, 1000, 1100, 1152, 1200, 1279 and 1280
findings.problem: Everything from 701px to 1279px renders a composition that has never been drawn. .b-two resolves to one track across the whole band: 960px at 1152, 1068px at 1279. Three things break in it at once. The horizon is position: static at every width below 1280 and position: sticky at 1280 and up, so the lock's own promise - the day is a horizon that never moves, and at desk width the count, the date and what the day is stop scrolling - is false for the 579px band most unmaximised laptop windows sit in. .b-todayRule, the single indigo mark on the owner's screen, is bound to its column, so it measures 344px at 1280 and 1440, 576px at 768, 960px at 1152 and 1068px at 1279: a factor of three, and at the top of the band it is a full-bleed rule running the whole page under the date, which reads as a section divider rather than as today. And the first moment on the plan sits at y941 at 1152 against y574 at 1280, so on a 1152x800 window the entire viewport is the bar, the count, the date, one sentence and an empty rail - none of the plan the owner came to see. frames.json holds 390, 768, 1280 and 1440 only, which is exactly why this survived four rounds: the band has never been rendered by the build, screenshotted, or looked at by any seat.
findings.fix: Split the two-column composition where it actually works rather than at the width the editor needs. In b.css change the desk query from min-width: 1280px to min-width: 1000px for three things only - .b-two's grid-template-columns, the horizon column's position: sticky, and the measure's padding-left - and leave the editor's own rules on min-width: 1280px so the editor stays a sheet below 1280 exactly as decided. For the 701-999 band, which is then the only single-column desk band, pin the accent to the horizon rather than to the column: .b-todayRule { width: 344px; max-width: 100% }. Add 1152 to the width list in frames.json and to the shot matrix so the band renders on every build and no round can miss it again.

findings.element: .b-measureHead's 22px margin-top against .b-who in every two-column state, measured at 1280 and 1440 on owner-flight, owner-editing, desk and print
findings.problem: Both columns of the composition open with the same object: an 11px mono uppercase micro-label. MARA & FINN heads the horizon, DAYS AWAY heads the measure. Same size, same weight, same tracking, same colour, same job, first ink in their column, and the eye reads them as a pair because there is nothing else at that altitude. They are 22px apart in every two-column state at every desk width, and it is the same 22 every time: .b-who tops at y235 and .b-measureHead at y257 on owner-flight at both 1280 and 1440; 116 against 138 on desk; 124 against 146 on print. The cause is .b-measureHead's 22px margin-top, which is right on the phone, where the head follows the horizon down one column and needs air above it, and which is inherited unchanged into the mediums where the grid row already supplies the top. So the same label is a follower on the phone and a column head on the desk, and it is styled as a follower in both. This is the class of thing that passes every gate mathematically and tells a reader optically that the page was assembled rather than composed.
findings.fix: Zero it where the label heads a column instead of following one. In b.css, inside the min-width desk block, add [data-medium="sheet"] .b-measureHead, [data-medium="full"] .b-measureHead { margin-top: 0 }. Both labels are the same size and weight, so flush tops means flush baselines. Driven to verify: .b-who and .b-measureHead both open at y235 at 1280 and 1440, and the measure column lifts 22px, which also pulls the printed sheet 22px shorter. Assert it in interaction-check.mjs: in any state where .b-two resolves to two tracks, .b-who and .b-measureHead share a bounding-box top within 1px.

findings.element: --gap-hair through --gap-page (shell.css:84-92) against every rendered block margin and padding in b.css
findings.problem: Round 4's ladder was declared and then not applied, and nothing in the system can tell. Nine steps exist - 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 28, 40, 56, 80 - and driving all eleven states at 390 and 1440 and reading every rendered non-control block margin-top, margin-bottom, padding-top and padding-bottom returns 47 distinct declarations that are on none of them: .b-who at 14, 18 and 22; .b-count at 6 and 10; .b-todayRule at 18 and 26; .b-measure at 10 and 14; .b-gapNote at 10 and 14; .b-measureHead at 22; .b-field padding at 26, 30 and 48; .b-print at 26, 30 and 44; .b-endedTitle at 14; .b-endedBody at 24; .b-bar at 18 and 24; .b-og at 18; .b-unfurlMeta and .b-bubble at 10; .b-behindRows at 6; .b-sub at 26; .b-skel at 10; .b-printLink at 30. Neither audit.mjs nor interaction-check.mjs mentions the tokens, so the ladder is a comment: it cannot fail, and it is not failing. The phone-to-desk compression pairs the round-4 refuter protected - 14/6/18/10/10 against 22/10/26/14/14 - are a real ratio worth keeping, but that is the argument for a second declared scale, not for ten raw numbers retyped by hand. Finding three above is the direct cost: 22 belongs to no ladder, does one job correctly on the phone and a different, wrong job on the desk, and nothing in the system could notice.
findings.fix: Declare the compression as a scale and then gate both. In shell.css add five paired steps beneath the nine, commented as the phone compression of 8/12/16/20/28: --gap-hair2: 6px, --gap-tight2: 10px, --gap-line2: 14px, --gap-item2: 18px, --gap-block2: 26px. Re-key b.css:1104-1109 and 1125-1130 to the pairs so the ratio is stated once rather than retyped; set .b-field padding to var(--gap-block2) var(--gap-item) var(--gap-section) and its sheet override to var(--gap-major) var(--gap-page) var(--gap-section); .b-endedTitle to var(--gap-line2); .b-endedBody to var(--gap-block2); .b-bar to var(--gap-item2) and var(--gap-block2); .b-og, .b-unfurlMeta and .b-bubble to var(--gap-item2) and var(--gap-tight2); .b-sub and .b-printLink to var(--gap-block2); .b-behindRows to var(--gap-hair2). Then gate it in audit.mjs alongside the type ramp: read every rendered non-control block margin-top/bottom and padding-top/bottom across all eleven states at all four widths and fail on any value outside the fourteen-step set, exempting controls by role exactly as the leading ladder already does.

findings.element: the split between shell.css (282 lines, no timeline noun in it) and b.css (1201 lines, 101 .b-* classes, every one a timeline noun), against the requirement at brief.md:68
findings.problem: The brief says whatever wins must be extractable as a small named language - materials, type, motion, composition - that Home, Notes and Tasks can wear next. Half of it is genuinely done. shell.css declares seven ladders - ink, paper, the fore/back pair, tracking, leading, space, radii and motion - plus the stage and the four media, and not one of them mentions a wedding, a plan or a day. A second product can inherit all of it tomorrow at no cost. The composition half does not exist as a language at all. Every rule a second product would actually need is written inside a timeline-named selector and cannot be referenced without copying the file: the field and its medium-bound insets, the rule-topped section rhythm stated in prose at b.css:322 and then retyped per section, the 11px mono uppercase micro-label that is the single most repeated object in the whole design and has no name, the foot, the 35px action, the convention that anything unbuilt gets inert text and no button element, the two-track stage split, the compression pairs. Build Notes from what is here and you fork b.css and rename 101 classes, at which point the two products drift apart on the first fix either of them takes. lock.md names the direction, the ground decision and the organising object; it names no object of the language. So the honest answer to the question this round asked is no: a second product can be built from the materials, and cannot be built from the composition without copying this one.
findings.fix: Extract one file and one page, both small, before any of this reaches Home. Create language.css between shell.css and b.css declaring eight objects by generic name, each lifted verbatim from the b.css rule that already exists: .sig-field (the medium-bound page inset), .sig-section (border-top plus the 40-above/20-below rhythm), .sig-label (11px mono uppercase, --track-label, --fore-46, 2px pad), .sig-title, .sig-sub, .sig-foot, .sig-act (the 35px control), .sig-inert (unbuilt things are text, never a button). Reduce b.css's equivalents to pairings in render-b.js - h("p.sig-label.b-who") rather than .b-who redeclaring the label - so Timeline keeps its nouns and the language owns the rules. Add one page to lock.md headed The language, listing the eight objects, the seven ladders and the four media with a line each. Then prove it: rebuild states.ended, which is four objects and no timeline logic, using only shell.css and language.css, and show it renders pixel-identical. If it does, Notes gets built from the page; if it does not, the page names what is still missing.

biggestWin: The instrument is right and the fixed round-4 items are genuinely fixed - I re-drove all of them. The accent has moved onto the live block on the morning (.b-dayNow's border-top computes rgb(79,70,229) and is the only indigo on the screen), the ended screen stands on the same 22px edge as its siblings, the loading frame no longer moves the one line the reader could already read, and the morning's sibling sections now sit on one 40/20 pair instead of 70/40/34. The measure remains the best thing here: the proportion between one gap and the next is exact at every scale I drove (98/196 at fourteen pixels a day, 126/252 at eighteen, identical ratio), and the keyboard model is disciplined in a way most shipped products never reach - the wedding morning is exactly one tab stop, owner-flight is eleven with every accessible name carrying the moment it belongs to, and nothing invisible is focusable. What is missing is that composition has only ever been checked at the four widths the build renders, and this round I looked at the two places nobody had. Both fail. At true A4 the keepsake is a single stacked column that needs two sheets and puts the wedding day on the back, because a container query threshold sits sixteen pixels above the width A4 actually gives it - the printed object has never been produced, only pictured at 1440. And the 579px band from 701 to 1279, where most unmaximised laptop windows live, renders a one-column layout in which the locked promise that the horizon stops scrolling is simply false and the one indigo mark becomes a full-bleed page rule. Neither is a decision to reopen and neither is a rebuild. Distance to 9.5: the A4 is a threshold, a padding value, an @page block and a gate, about a day; the band is one breakpoint moved from 1280 to 1000 plus one width added to frames.json, half a day; the column heads are one line; the space ladder is a half-day of re-keying plus one assertion. The extractable language is the only item that is a build rather than polish, and it is small - one 150-line file, one page of lock.md, one state rebuilt as proof, call it two days - but it is the item the founder should care about most, because Timeline went first specifically so the next three products could wear what it produced, and what it currently produces is materials plus a fork. The score is 7.8 rather than round 4's 8.1 because the surfaces that had been looked at got better and the two that had not are worse than anything in round 4: a keepsake that prints on two sheets and a laptop band that shows none of the plan are not shipped work, and neither of them was visible in a single frame this panel has ever been given.
